title: 1 Samuel 20:24–34
context: At the new moon meal, David’s seat is empty. Saul assumes ritual uncleanness the first day, but on the second asks about ‘the son of Jesse.’ When Jonathan gives the agreed excuse, Saul insults him, insists that David must die for the sake of Jonathan’s kingdom, and hurls a spear at his own son. Jonathan leaves in grief and anger. Both traditions read the scene with moral clarity about Saul’s jealousy and as shared ground about Jonathan’s costly loyalty.

verses.text: So David hid himself in the field. When the new moon had come, the king sat himself down to eat food.
verses.arminianNotes:
David hides in the field, and when the new moon comes, the king sits down to eat. The plan is set in motion.

Arminian readers see both friends carrying out their parts faithfully.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrative shifts to the king’s table. Tension builds.

Reformed readers see events unfolding under God’s watch. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground, with the meal scene set to reveal Saul’s true intentions toward David, as the friends had planned in the field.

verses.text: The king sat on his seat, as at other times, even on the seat by the wall; and Jonathan stood up, and Abner sat by Saul’s side, but David’s place was empty.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul sits in his usual seat by the wall, Abner beside him, Jonathan present, and David’s place empty. The seating is described carefully.

Arminian readers see the empty seat as the silent center of the scene.
verses.reformedNotes:
The detail emphasizes the formality of the meal. David’s absence is conspicuous.

Reformed readers see the narrative focusing on what is missing. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with the empty seat silently raising the question the next verses answer.

verses.text: Nevertheless Saul didn’t say anything that day, for he thought, “Something has happened to him. He is not clean. Surely he is not clean.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul says nothing the first day, assuming David is ceremonially unclean. Ritual uncleanness would keep someone from a sacred meal.

Arminian readers see Saul giving a plausible explanation for the absence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Saul’s assumption reflects the purity laws, such as those of Leviticus 7:20–21. He waits a day.

Reformed readers see the narrative building suspense. Both traditions read this plainly as shared ground and note that ritual uncleanness here is not a moral charge against David.

verses.text: On the next day after the new moon, the second day, David’s place was empty. Saul said to Jonathan his son, “Why didn’t the son of Jesse come to eat, either yesterday, or today?”
verses.arminianNotes:
On the second day, Saul asks Jonathan why the son of Jesse has not come. He uses a dismissive title.

Arminian readers see Saul’s hostility surfacing in his choice of words.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calling David ‘the son of Jesse’ rather than by name may signal contempt. Saul’s patience ends.

Reformed readers see the question opening the way for Saul’s anger. Both traditions read this as shared ground, noting the narrative’s attention to the tone of Saul’s speech.

verses.text: Jonathan answered Saul, “David earnestly asked permission of me to go to Bethlehem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan answers that David asked permission to go to Bethlehem. He delivers the agreed explanation.

Arminian readers see Jonathan keeping his promise to David under pressure, even before an angry king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan repeats the cover story from verse 6. He stands with his friend.

Reformed readers see faithful loyalty in a dangerous moment. Both traditions read this plainly, narrating the excuse without endorsing it, and note the courage required to speak it to an angry king.

verses.text: He said, ‘Please let me go, for our family has a sacrifice in the city. My brother has commanded me to be there. Now, if I have found favor in your eyes, please let me go away and see my brothers.’ Therefore he has not come to the king’s table.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan adds David’s supposed words about a family sacrifice and his brother’s command. The explanation is detailed.

Arminian readers note that the narrative presents this as the agreed cover, without approving the deception.
verses.reformedNotes:
The excuse is elaborated to sound plausible. Its truth is not confirmed by the narrative.

Reformed readers likewise read it plainly. Both traditions treat the account as narration within a crisis, not as a commendation of the ruse, and as shared ground.

verses.text: Then Saul’s anger burned against Jonathan, and he said to him, “You son of a perverse rebellious woman, don’t I know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame, and to the shame of your mother’s nakedness?
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul’s anger burns, and he insults Jonathan and his mother, accusing him of choosing David to his own shame. His words are harsh.

Arminian readers see jealousy turning into cruelty even toward his own son.
verses.reformedNotes:
Saul’s insult is coarse and humiliating. His rage targets Jonathan’s loyalty.

Reformed readers see how sin distorts family relationships. Both traditions read this with moral clarity and without sensationalism, recognizing the pain Jonathan endures for his friendship.

verses.text: For as long as the son of Jesse lives on the earth, you will not be established, nor will your kingdom. Therefore now send and bring him to me, for he shall surely die!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul tells Jonathan that as long as David lives, Jonathan’s kingdom will not be secure, and demands that David be brought to die. Dynasty is Saul’s concern.

Arminian readers see Saul clinging to power God has already taken from him (15:28).
verses.reformedNotes:
Saul sees David as a threat to his line. He refuses to accept God’s word through Samuel.

Reformed readers see resistance to God’s purpose. Both traditions read this as shared ground, contrasting Saul’s grasping with Jonathan’s willing acceptance of David’s future.

verses.text: Jonathan answered Saul his father, and said to him, “Why should he be put to death? What has he done?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan asks why David should die and what he has done. He defends his friend again.

Arminian readers see courage in standing for the innocent even before an enraged king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan’s questions echo 19:4–5. He presses for justice.

Reformed readers see faithful advocacy that risks everything. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground and honor Jonathan’s persistent defense of David’s innocence, which now puts his own life in danger.

verses.text: Saul cast his spear at him to strike him. By this Jonathan knew that his father was determined to put David to death.
verses.arminianNotes:
Saul throws his spear at Jonathan, and Jonathan knows his father is determined to kill David. The truth is now plain.

Arminian readers see Saul’s violence revealing his settled intent.
verses.reformedNotes:
Saul’s attack on his own son mirrors his attacks on David. The test has given its answer.

Reformed readers see the depth of Saul’s rebellion. Both traditions read this as shared ground and with moral clarity about the danger Saul’s jealousy now poses to everyone near him.

verses.text: So Jonathan arose from the table in fierce anger, and ate no food the second day of the month; for he was grieved for David, because his father had treated him shamefully.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jonathan leaves the table in fierce anger and eats nothing the second day, grieved for David and shamed by his father. His grief is for his friend.

Arminian readers see righteous anger and deep sorrow mingled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jonathan fasts in grief. His anger reflects both injustice to David and his father’s insult.

Reformed readers see righteous indignation joined with love. Both traditions read this as shared ground, honoring Jonathan’s grief and his refusal to share in his father’s plan.
